title: The Plot to Seize Krishna; Satyaki's Alarm
story:
Some conspiracies are born in whispers so low that the walls themselves seem to lean in to listen. The one that took shape in Hastinapura began when Duryodhana, eldest of the Kuru princes, rose from the assembly and walked out in anger, deaf to the grave words his mother had just spoken to him, and went to the company of men who would tell him only what he wanted to hear.

Krishna had come to that court as the messenger of the five Pandavas, his friends, who had lost their kingdom to their cousins in a rigged game of dice and now stood at the edge of war. He came to ask for peace. The blind king Dhritarashtra, the grandsire Bhishma, and the wise Vidura had all urged Duryodhana to accept what he offered. He would not. And now, outside the assembly, with the dust of the court still settling behind him, he set his mind to the other way of ending the matter.

He consulted Sakuni, Suvala's son, the man most clever at dice — the same Sakuni who had once gambled the Pandavas' kingdom away from them. Karna joined them, and Dussasana made the fourth. "Krishna is quick to act," they told one another. "With Dhritarashtra and Bhishma behind him, he hopes to move against us first. Then we shall seize him before he can stir — as Indra once seized the mighty Vali."

Each of them added reasons, and each reason sounded, to their own ears, like wisdom. Once Krishna was bound, the Pandavas would lose heart and become helpless, like snakes whose fangs had been broken. He was the refuge and protection of them all — the giver of boons, the pride of his whole people. Confine him, and the Pandavas and their allies would sit crushed and useless. So, deaf to Dhritarashtra's protests, they would take him then and there, in the heart of the Kuru court, and fight the war they wanted afterwards.

What the four conspirators did not know was that they had already been read. Satyaki, Krishna's companion, could tell a man's heart by his signs — the too-quick glance, the careful lowering of a voice, the way Duryodhana's fingers worked at the hilt of his sword as he spoke of seizure. He knew the plot before the plotters had finished shaping it. He rose quietly and left the court, with Kritavarman, son of Hridika, at his side.

At the entrance he stopped and turned. "Array your troops in mail," he told Kritavarman, "and wait here at the door of the court until I have put this matter before Krishna."

Then Satyaki went back into the hall like a lion entering a mountain cave. He told Krishna first, then king Dhritarashtra, then Vidura. And when he had set the whole plot before them, he laughed.

"These men mean to do a thing here that no good man could approve," he said, "and they call it virtue, gain, and desire. They will never manage it. They are fools burning with anger and greed, and they think to seize the lotus-eyed one — as if children tried to catch a blazing fire in their clothes."

Vidura, who could see far ahead, turned to Dhritarashtra in the midst of the Kurus. "King, the hour of all your sons has come," he said. "They are set on a shameful act that they cannot accomplish. United, they hope to overpower Krishna — but if he wished, he could send every one of them, even fighting together, to the land of the dead, as an angry lion scatters a herd of elephants. They will perish like insects in a fire. Yet he will do nothing wrongful, not even now. This man will never swerve from virtue."

In the doorway stood Kritavarman's mail-clad ranks, silent and ready. In the middle of the hall sat the man they had meant to seize — untouched, unhurried, listening. And in the hush that followed Vidura's words, everyone present understood what quarry the four had chosen, and that the conspiracy was dead before it had ever been allowed to move.
reflection: The conspiracy fails at the moment of its forming, and not because the plotters were careless: they simply misjudged the company they kept. Duryodhana counted on deceiving everyone in the court, but he sat within reach of a man who could read hearts by signs, and he plotted against someone who did not need an army to be unseizable.
next_story_tease: When Krishna heard the warning, his answer would be neither fear nor anger, but a calm permission that unsettled the conspirators more than any threat.
hero_scene: Satyaki strides back into the Kuru assembly like a lion entering a mountain cave, while Kritavarman's mail-clad troops wait in silence at the court's entrance.
